value: 180 days from receipt of the adverse benefit determination notice to file an internal appeal
notes: healthcare.gov: file the internal appeal within 180 days (6 months) of receiving notice that the claim was denied. The underlying rule is 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(i) (plans must allow at least 180 days following receipt of notification of an adverse benefit determination), which 45 CFR 147.136 extends to non-grandfathered individual and group coverage; the 2560.503-1 text was confirmed on govinfo.gov (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol9/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol9-sec2560-503-1.xml). The ecfr.gov and govinfo copies of 45 CFR 147.136 could not be fetched in this session (bot block / 404).
sourceQuote: file your internal appeal within 180 days (6 months) of receiving notice

value: 4 months after receiving the insurer's final internal appeal denial to request an external review
notes: healthcare.gov: a written external review request must be filed within 4 months after the date the consumer receives the notice or final determination from the insurer (roughly 120 days). External reviewer decision deadlines on the same page: standard review no later than 45 days after the request is received; expedited review no later than 72 hours (or less depending on medical urgency). The federal external review rule is 45 CFR 147.136(d); its regulation text could not be fetched in this session.
sourceQuote: within 4 months after the date you receive a notice or final determination

value: Internal appeal decision deadlines: urgent care 72 hours; pre-service (service not yet received) 30 days; post-service (service already received) 60 days
notes: healthcare.gov states the internal appeal must be completed within 30 days for a service not yet received and within 60 days for a service already received. For urgent care the healthcare.gov page says the decision must come as quickly as the medical condition requires and at least within 4 business days after the request is received, whereas the regulation it is based on, 29 CFR 2560.503-1(i)(2)(i) (confirmed on govinfo.gov), requires a decision as soon as possible and not later than 72 hours after receipt of the request for review; the 72-hour figure is the regulatory standard and the 4-business-day wording is the consumer page's description. Under 2560.503-1(i)(2)(ii)-(iii), plans that use two appeal levels get 15 days (pre-service) and 30 days (post-service) per level. External review decisions: standard within 45 days, expedited within 72 hours (healthcare.gov external review page).
sourceQuote: Your internal appeal must be completed within 30 days

value: 65 calendar days from the date of the plan's notice of the organization determination to request a reconsideration (level 1 appeal)
notes: cms.gov (Part C reconsideration page) and medicare.gov (Appeals in Medicare health plans, https://www.medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/medicare-health-plans) both currently state 65 days from the date on the notice. Older regulation text (42 CFR 422.582(b), 2010 CFR edition on govinfo) said 60 calendar days from the date of the notice. The CY2025 Medicare Advantage/Part D final rule (Federal Register, April 23, 2024, document 2024-07105) revised 422.582 so the 60-day period runs from receipt of the notice, with receipt presumed 5 calendar days after the notice date, which CMS now expresses as 65 calendar days from the notice date; search excerpts indicate CMS finalized the revision as proposed, but the exact effective date of the change was not confirmed from fetched text (the rule covers contract year 2025). Late requests must give a reason for filing late (good cause). Plan decision deadlines on the cms.gov page: 30 calendar days for standard pre-service requests, 60 calendar days for payment requests, 72 hours for expedited pre-service or Part B drug requests. The same 65-day window applies to Part D redeterminations.
sourceQuote: within 65 calendar days from the date of the notice of the organization determination

value: 3 consecutive months (commonly described as a 90-day grace period) for Marketplace enrollees receiving the premium tax credit who have paid at least one full month's premium in the benefit year; the grace period for enrollees not using the premium tax credit is set by state law or the plan
notes: healthcare.gov glossary: the grace period is usually 3 months if the enrollee has a Marketplace plan and uses the premium tax credit and has paid at least one full month's premium during the benefit year; it states the length may be different for enrollees who do not use the premium tax credit. The page says 3 months rather than 90 days; the 90-day figure is the common restatement. The governing regulation is 45 CFR 156.270(d) (three consecutive months); the ecfr.gov and govinfo copies could not be fetched in this session. The commonly cited 30-day grace period for unsubsidized enrollees was not confirmed from a fetched source and varies by state.
sourceQuote: usually 3 months if both of the following are true

value: 30-day free look period after receiving a new Medigap policy
notes: medicare.gov: if you buy a new Medigap policy you have to cancel your old policy, except during your 30-day free look period; medicare.gov guidance (search excerpt) is to keep the first policy until deciding to keep the second, paying both premiums for that month, because a cancelled Medigap policy cannot be reinstated. Medicare SELECT buyers have 12 months to switch to a standard Medigap policy (medicare.gov search excerpt).

value: At least 10 days is the common state minimum; several states require 14 to 30 days (e.g., New York 10 to 30 days with 30 days for mail-order policies; Texas at least 10 to 20 days; Florida at least 14 days; California 30 days for seniors)
notes: Texas Department of Insurance life insurance guide: Texas policies have a free-look period of at least 10 to 20 days, during which the policy can be cancelled for any reason for a full refund. Search excerpts from other state pages: New York DFS life insurance FAQ (minimum 10 days, maximum 30 days; 30 days required for policies sold by mail; https://www.dfs.ny.gov/faqs/consumer_faqs/life_insurance), Washington OIC (10-day free look on every new life policy; https://www.insurance.wa.gov/insurance-resources/life-insurance/learn-how-life-insurance-works), South Carolina DOI (no less than 10 days; 30-day review for mail-order policies; https://www.doi.sc.gov/FAQ.aspx?QID=332), Florida DFS life insurance guide (free look of at least 14 days), California DOI Senior Insurance Bill of Rights (30 days for life, annuity, long-term care and Medicare supplement policies bought by seniors; https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0150-seniors/0600informationguides/Informing-Senior.cfm). The free-look notice is normally printed on the policy cover page. The claim that replacement policies commonly carry a 30-day free look was not confirmed from a fetched source.
sourceQuote: Texas policies have a free-look period of at least 10 to 20 days.

value: 31-day grace period after the premium due date is standard (30 days in some states); coverage continues during the grace period and a death benefit paid during it is reduced by the unpaid premium
notes: Texas Department of Insurance life insurance guide: most policies have a 31-day grace period after the premium due date; the premium can be paid during the grace period with no interest while coverage continues; if the premium is not paid within the grace period the policy lapses. Florida DFS life insurance guide (search excerpt, https://www.myfloridacfo.com/docs-sf/consumer-services-libraries/consumerservices-documents/understanding-coverage/consumer-guides/life-insurance-guide.pdf): right to a 30-day grace period during which the policy remains in force. State standard-provision statutes set the minimum; no specific statute was fetched.
sourceQuote: Most policies have a 31-day grace period after your premium's due date.

value: Insurer-initiated cancellation: unearned premium is refunded pro-rata (in proportion to the unexpired policy term). Insured-initiated cancellation: the insurer may calculate the refund on a short-rate basis (retaining more than the pro-rata share, roughly 10% of the unexpired premium, or charging a flat fee) unless state law or the policy requires a pro-rata refund.
notes: New York DFS consumer page (direct fetch was blocked; content taken from search-engine excerpts of the page): in general, if an insurer cancels a policy, premiums are returned on a pro-rata basis; when the insured cancels, some insurers calculate the refund on a short-rate basis, meaning the insurer retains a greater portion of the premium than pro-rata, on average about 10% of the unexpired portion of the premium and more if the policy is cancelled early in the term. Florida DFS personal auto overview (search excerpt, https://www.myfloridacfo.com/division/consumers/understanding-insurance/personal-automobile-insurance-overview): when the company cancels it must refund 100% of the unearned premium within 15 days of the cancellation date; when the insured cancels the insurer may keep 10% of the unearned premium (short rate), except service members called to active duty receive a full refund. Texas DOI auto guide (https://www.tdi.texas.gov/pubs/consumer/cb020.html): the company must refund any unearned premium within 15 days after the cancellation date; a 2025 TDI rule adoption (search excerpt of https://www.tdi.texas.gov/rules/2025/documents/20269730.pdf) requires pro-rata refunds for personal auto, subject to a minimum retained premium. Massachusetts guidance (search excerpt): no short-rate penalty for cancelling an auto policy in the first 30 days. Premium-financed policies generally must be refunded pro-rata (NY DFS OGC opinions). Pro-rata refund = premium x (days remaining / days in term).
sourceQuote: if an insurer cancels a policy, premiums are returned on a pro-rata basis

value: Advance written notice is required before an insurer cancels; Texas requires 10 days' notice for any permitted reason; New York requires 15 days' notice for nonpayment of premium and 20 days for other permitted grounds; other states vary
notes: Texas Department of Insurance auto insurance guide: a company must give 10 days' notice before it cancels a policy; after the first 60 days it may cancel only for nonpayment of premium, a fraudulent claim, or a suspended or revoked driver's license or registration (the first 60 days it may cancel for any lawful reason); unearned premium must be refunded within 15 days of the cancellation date. New York DFS (search excerpt of https://www.dfs.ny.gov/consumers/auto_insurance/cancellation_and_renewal): a permitted mid-term cancellation notice must be sent at least 20 days before the effective date, or 15 days if nonpayment of premium is the ground, and a nonpayment notice must clearly state the amount due. Required notice periods differ by state and by reason; check the state DOI page or the policy's cancellation condition.
sourceQuote: A company must give you 10 days' notice before it cancels your policy.

jurisdiction: US, varies by state (NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices model)
value: Acknowledge the claim within 15 days of notice; accept or deny within a fixed period after proof of loss (NAIC model regulation: 21 days; California: 40 calendar days); if more time is needed, send written status letters (NAIC model: every 45 days; California: every 30 days); pay accepted claims promptly (California: within 30 days)
notes: California Department of Insurance consumer guide (official page; wording per search excerpt): insurers must accept or deny a claim immediately but in no event later than 40 days after receiving proof of claim (10 CCR 2695.7(b)), and must send written notice of any additional information needed if more time is required. Regulation text (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 10, read via Cornell LII: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-2695.5 and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-2695.7): acknowledge receipt, provide forms and begin investigation within 15 calendar days of notice of claim (2695.5(e)); respond to claimant communications within 15 calendar days (2695.5(b)); accept or deny within 40 calendar days of proof of claim (2695.7(b)); written status notice every 30 calendar days if the claim cannot be decided within 40 days (2695.7(c)(1)); pay accepted claims within 30 calendar days (2695.7(h)); the CDI index of these regulations is at https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/130-laws-regs-hearings/05-CCR/fair-claims-regs.cfm. NAIC Unfair Property/Casualty Claims Settlement Practices Model Regulation (MDL-902, July 1997 text, https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-902.pdf, read from the downloaded PDF): Section 6A, acknowledge receipt of a claim within 15 days unless paid within that time; Section 6C, reply to other pertinent communications within 15 days; Section 7A, advise the first-party claimant of acceptance or denial within 21 days after receipt of properly executed proofs of loss, or notify within 21 days that more time is needed, then send letters 45 days from initial notification and every 45 days thereafter. The model regulation says 15 days (not 15 working days); state adoptions vary, so check the state's version.

value: 180 days after receipt of the adverse benefit determination to appeal a denied disability claim; the plan must decide the appeal within 45 days, extendable once by up to 45 days for special circumstances if written notice is given before the initial period ends
notes: 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(4) applies the 180-day appeal period of (h)(3)(i) to disability claims. Paragraph (i)(3)(i) applies the (i)(1)(i) timeframe with 45 days substituted for 60 days, giving a 45-day decision period and one extension of up to 45 days (the base (i)(1)(i) rule is 60 days plus one extension of up to 60 days; the fetched text does not spell out the extension length for disability claims separately, so the 45-day extension is derived from the substitution). Group health plan appeal deadlines in (i)(2): 72 hours urgent care, 30 days pre-service, 60 days post-service (15 and 30 days per level where two appeal levels are used). Regulation text read from the 2024 CFR edition on govinfo.gov; ecfr.gov blocked automated fetching.
sourceQuote: at least 180 days following receipt of a notification of an adverse benefit determination

value: In states that adopted the NAIC Travel Insurance Model Act, the buyer may cancel for a full refund within at least 10 days after delivery of the fulfillment materials (15 days if delivered by postal mail), provided no covered trip has started and no claim has been filed; other states have no guaranteed window
notes: West Virginia Code 33-62-8(c)(3) (state enactment of the NAIC Travel Insurance Model Act): unless the insured has started a covered trip or filed a claim, the policyholder may cancel for a full refund of the travel protection plan price from purchase until at least 15 days following delivery of the fulfillment materials by postal mail, or 10 days following delivery by other means. Search excerpts show the same 15/10-day language in Rhode Island (27-79.1-8) and Iowa (515K.5) statutes, and a Center for Economic Justice comment letter to the NAIC attributes it to Section 7(C)(3) of the NAIC Travel Insurance Model Act (#632); the NAIC travel insurance topic page (search excerpt) reports the model was adopted in December 2018 and enacted by 38 states as of April 2026 (not independently verified). North Carolina DOI's consumer guide (https://www.ncdoi.gov/consumers-guide-travel-insurance/open) says a policy might provide a short free-look period and to check the deadline, so in non-adopting states the window depends on the policy. The NAIC model act text itself was not fetched.
sourceQuote: Ten days following the date of delivery of the travel protection plan's fulfillment materials

value: NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act: 15 days from receipt of the policy to return it for a refund unless a claim has been filed; California requires a free-look period of not less than 30 days (Cal. Ins. Code 12880.2); other states vary
notes: NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act (#633, Summer 2022 text; search excerpt of https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/MO633.pdf): unless the insured has filed a claim, applicants have the right to examine and return the policy, certificate or rider within 15 days of receipt, and the required notice reads that the buyer has 15 days from the day of receipt to review and return it; an earlier NAIC discussion draft had said not less than 30 days. California Insurance Code 12880.2 (enacted by AB 2056, 2014; enrolled bill text at https://www.leginfo.ca.gov/pub/13-14/bill/asm/ab_2051-2100/ab_2056_bill_20140820_enrolled.htm; current codified text via FindLaw at https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/insurance-code/ins-sect-12880-2/): the policy must carry a notice that it may be returned for cancellation, the free-look period must be not less than 30 days, returning it voids the policy from the start with premium refunded within 30 days of notice of cancellation, and the right does not apply once a claim has been paid or the insurer has agreed in writing to pay one. The official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov code page blocked automated fetching, so the current California wording rests on the 2014 enrolled bill and a secondary code site. A trade-press claim that most states use a 30-day pet free look was not verified.
sourceQuote: within fifteen (15) days of its receipt

value: If the insurer will not refund a duplicate premium charge: for a credit card, send a written billing-error dispute to the card issuer within 60 calendar days after the statement showing the charge (Fair Credit Billing Act / Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.13); for a debit card or bank-account (ACH) debit, notify the bank within 60 days after it sent the statement showing the error (Electronic Fund Transfer Act / Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.11)
notes: CFPB, credit cards: call the issuer, then send a written billing-error notice to the billing-error address on the statement within 60 calendar days after the charge appeared on the statement; the issuer must acknowledge in writing within 30 days (unless already resolved) and resolve the dispute within two complete billing cycles and no more than 90 days after receiving the notice; the disputed amount and related finance charges need not be paid while the dispute is pending; if the issuer agrees it must remove the charge, otherwise it must explain in writing (sources: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-a-charge-on-my-credit-card-bill-en-61/ and https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/credit-cards/how-to-fix-mistakes-in-your-credit-card-bill/). CFPB, bank accounts and debit cards (search excerpts of https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-my-money-back-after-i-discover-an-unauthorized-transaction-or-money-missing-from-my-bank-account-en-1017/ and Regulation E 12 CFR 1005.11 at https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/11/): notify the bank within 60 days after it sends the statement showing the error; the bank generally has 10 business days to investigate (20 for accounts open under 30 days) and must provisionally credit the account if it needs longer, with up to 45 days (90 for point-of-sale, foreign or new-account transactions) to resolve. Card network rules can be stricter (some count 60 days from the transaction date), so act on the earlier date. Complaints can be filed at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or (855) 411-2372. Use this only after asking the insurer for the refund first; the dispute is with the card issuer or bank, not the insurer.
sourceQuote: within 60 calendar days after the charge appeared on your statement
